            Description
            This study conducted a matched meta-evaluation of 119 pairs of original research articles (Registered Reports [RRs] vs. traditional non-registered reports [non-RRs]) across 33 psychology journals, matching them by publication venue, time, and research topic. The findings indicate that while RRs are designed to improve scientific transparency and reduce bias, they have not yet garnered higher academic or public attention compared to traditional reports; in fact, RRs were found to receive relatively fewer citations.
          
        

        
        
          
            My Responsibilities
            When I first joined this project, it was nothing more than a rough concept with no existing roadmap to follow. I brainstormed several analytical approaches and created the visualizations that clearly highlight how RRs and non-RRs differ across various dimensions. I wrote over 95% of the code and drafted the entire Methods and Results sections. Regarding the Introduction and Discussion sections, I proposed several potential narrative directions and thematic outlines grounded in the results we obtained. I also took the lead in addressing the statistical concerns raised by the reviewers during the peer-review process.

            Description
            Although the Self-Matching Task exhibits highly robust effects at the group level, its individual-level reliability (both split-half and test-retest reliability) remains relatively low. This further corroborates the existence of the reliability paradox in cognitive paradigms.
          
        

        
        
          
            My Responsibilities
            I assumed nearly all responsibilities for the project's workflow. I managed the end-to-end process of data curation—scouring databases for open data and coordinating with authors for raw datasets. I also handled the rigorous side of open science by writing the pre-registration and the manuscript itself. To ensure our analysis was robust, I also built two R packages specifically for our split-half reliability metrics and executed the entire analysis pipeline.

            Reinforcement learning often poses a high barrier for psychologists due to the complexity of building MDPs and writing low-level code. By using simple if-else logic to define cognitive processes, researchers can easily execute a complete pipeline—from model construction and parameter recovery to fitting and visualization.               Updated on Apr 23, 2026
            
          
          
          
          
            
            
              
                 GitHub
              
            
            
          
        

        
        
          
            Description
            A recent reanalysis by Collins (2025) suggests that learning in the RLWM paradigm is driven by Habit (H) and Working Memory (WM), rather than a slow RL process. This project uses the custom multiRL R package to re-implement these models, progressing from simple (RL, WM, H) to complex mixtures to test parameter redundancy and recoverability. Results show that a parsimonious 3-parameter HWM model sufficiently recovers key experimental effects, while adding parameters degrades performance, strongly supporting Occam's razor. Furthermore, benchmarking MLE, ABC, and RNN reveals that ABC yields the best parameter recovery for this paradigm.

              Started on Dec 5, 2023
            
          
          
          
          
            
              
                 DOI
              
            
            
              
                 GitHub
              
            
            
          
        

        
        
          
            Description
            This three-level meta-analysis of 41 studies (N = 8376) reveals that business decision-making games significantly enhance training effectiveness with a moderate overall effect (g = 0.53). The games effectively improve reactions (g = 0.44), learning processes (g = 0.66), and performance (g = 0.45), with the strongest impact on trainee motivation (g = 0.85). These positive outcomes remain robust across various participant types, game designs, and academic fields, supporting the broad implementation of such games in business education.
          
        

        
        
          
            My Responsibilities
            I was responsible for developing the standardized workflow code for the meta-analysis.

            Description
            This study systematically examined the heterogeneity of depression scales for Chinese children and adolescents. Across 27 scales, we found substantial differences in symptom coverage and low overlap between instruments. Analyses of data from over 12,000 participants further showed that commonly used scales produced different detection rates and captured distinct symptom profiles. These findings suggest that youth depression scales are not interchangeable and highlight the need for culturally and developmentally adapted assessment tools in non-Western contexts.

            Description
            This project is a systematic, multi-level meta-analysis designed to synthesize empirical evidence regarding how newly acquired self-relevance modulates cognitive processes. While previous research often used pre-existing self-related stimuli (like one's own name or face), this study focuses on lab-based associative learning tasks, specifically the Self-Matching Task (SMT) and the Ownership Paradigm.
          
        

        
        
          
            My Responsibilities
            I joined this meta-analysis project following the initial coding of 136 papers using the Self-Perceptual Matching Task (SMT). I spearheaded the verification and cross-checking process for these studies and subsequently led the systematic search and coding efforts for newly published literature to ensure the project remained current. As the scope of the study expanded beyond its original goals to improve feasibility, I undertook a comprehensive overhaul of the technical infrastructure, rewriting the analytical code and restructuring the directory architecture. Currently, I continue to lead the project by providing training for new coders on evolving variables and developing R scripts for advanced statistical methodologies.

title: Beyond the Ten Simple Rules: Reliability, Validity, and Parsimony in Evaluating the RLWMH Models
text:
Figure: Human


Here’s my take on Collins (2025). In an MDP, two systems are involved: a reinforcement learning system and a working memory system. Within the reinforcement learning system, the process can be further differentiated into standard RL and Habit (H) based on whether the feedback is constantly treated as a subjective value of 1. The WM system consists of three parameters: the memory decay rate(zeta), working memory capacity, and the mixture weight between the RL and WM systems. Additionally, there are two system-independent parameters: sticky choice (action perseveration) and lapse rate (the probability of making an accidental motor error).


  


  


  


Figure: HWM(6-parameter)


First, I need to establish whether the model’s free parameters are recoverable. If a parameter isn’t recoverable, it suggests it may be redundant or effectively masked by other parameters. In this process, I found that, compared to the optimal HWM model proposed in Collins (2025), a streamlined three-parameter model shows better parameter recovery.


  


  


Figure: HWM(3-parameter)


Compared to the full six-parameter HWM model, the three-parameter model also does a better job reproducing the behavioral effects. However, it could be a misunderstanding on my part or a bug in the code. In any case, I’ll share any interesting findings here.

title: Registered Reports in Psychology Across Scholarly Citations and Public Dissemination: A Comparative Metaevaluation of More Than a Decade of Practice
text:
Registered Reports (RRs) represent a novel publishing format designed to enhance transparency and mitigate publication bias by conducting peer review before research outcomes are known. This meta-research identified 119 pairs of original research articles matched by journal, publication time, and research topic using keyword matching to compare their scholarly citations and public dissemination. Unfortunately, despite being viewed as a more rigorous publication model, RRs in psychology did not attract significantly higher attention; in fact, they were found to receive fewer scholarly citations than traditional non-registered reports.



In terms of scientific rigor, RRs demonstrated a clear advantage by significantly reducing the bias against null results, reporting positive findings at a rate of 62.83% compared to the much higher 85.84% found in traditional reports. Furthermore, transparency practices—including preregistration and the sharing of open data, code, and materials—were notably more prevalent in RRs than in their matched non-RR counterparts. However, this improved transparency and methodological quality did not translate into higher impact metrics, as RRs received lower citation counts when controlling for publication days, and overall public impact on social media remained statistically similar to traditional papers.



Because citation data is characterized by extreme positive skewness, we performed a detailed sensitivity analysis to ensure the findings were not driven by outliers. We systematically tested the stability of the results by removing different proportions of the most-cited articles and rerunning their analysis. This robustness check revealed that the finding of lower citation counts for RRs remained statistically significant unless more than 37% of the regression data or 50% of the F-test data were excluded, confirming that the citation disadvantage is a robust phenomenon within the studied sample.

Archived

These packages were developed to manage and analyze the large datasets involved in the Reliability of the Self‑Matching Task project. By packaging core functions, they avoid the messiness of traditional procedural scripts, facilitating both smooth project progression and reproducible research.




  
    
      
      
      

      
      
        
          yukiSH
          
            Archived
          
        
        
        
        
          
          
          
            
               GitHub
            
          
          
        
        

        
        
          
            This package is designed to split datasets according to input category variables (e.g., subject, experimental condition). It systematically applies four different split-half methods (Odd-Even, First-Second, Permuted Split-Half, and Monte Carlo Split-Half) to each sub-dataset, providing a standardized data foundation for subsequent reliability analysis.
          
        
      
    
  
    
      
      
      

      
      
        
          yukiBP
          
            Archived
          
        
        
        
        
          
          
          
            
               GitHub
            
          
          
        
        

        
        
          
            Working seamlessly with the split datasets generated by yukiSH, this package calculates split-half reliability across six key metrics: reaction time (RT), accuracy (ACC), efficiency (RT/ACC), d-prime, DDM drift rate (v), and DDM starting point (z). Since the computation process is highly parallelized across datasets, it dramatically accelerates the entire analytical workflow.

title: Mengzhen Hu (YuKi)
text:
Research Projects

Project 1

Beyond the Ten Simple Rules: Reliability, Validity, and Parsimony in Evaluating the RLWMH Models


 GitHub

In the field of computational modeling, various estimation methods are available to identify optimal parameter values for black-box functions. However, these methods often yield diverging estimates for the same model. To assess the robustness of different estimation methods, this project uses the open-access data and the RLWMH model from Collins (2025) as a case study. We provide a comprehensive benchmark of different estimation techniques. The goal of this research is to evaluate the stability of these estimation methods. Furthermore, we will systematically increase the number of free parameters, starting from the basic Rescorla-Wagner model and progressing toward the full RLWMH model. This incremental approach allows us to evaluate the model’s parsimony and identify potential parameter redundancy within the RLWMH framework proposed by Collins.


Project 2

binaryRL: Reinforcement Learning Modeling of Two-Alternative Forced Choice Decision Making in R—A Step-by-Step Tutorial.


 GitHub  OSF  DOI

Building reinforcement learning (RL) models can be a steep learning curve for many psychologists. To bridge this gap, we developed an R package that enables researchers to construct complex RL models using intuitive if-else logic. By providing a streamlined workflow, the package simplifies the entire process—from model specification to parameter estimation—making computational modeling accessible to all.


Project 3

Registered reports in psychology across scholarly citations and public dissemination: A comparative meta evaluation of more than a decade of practice


 GitHub  OSF  DOI

This project conducted a meta-analytical comparison of 120 pairs of Registered Reports (RRs) and non-Registered Reports (non-RRs) from 34 psychological journals, matched by journal, publication time, and research topic. It examined the academic recognition (citations) and public dissemination (Altmetric Attention Scores and Twitter posts) of RRs compared to traditional articles, controlling for factors like null-results reporting, transparency, and authorship.

Responsibility:

Coded collected articles, extracting key information.
Used lme4 to build hierarchical linear models to test for differences between RR and non-RR articles in citations and altmetrics, and to identify reasons for such differences.
Used Mplus to construct hierarchical linear models, examining whether journal impact factor moderates the relationship between article type (RR vs. non-RR) and dependent variables (e.g., citations and altmetrics).
Visualized the results using ggplot2.
Responded to reviewers’ statistical questions and provided solutions.
Authored the Methods and Results sections of the original draft.




Project 4

A multiverse assessment of the reliability of the self-matching task as a measurement of the self-prioritization effect


 GitHub  OSF  DOI

This project addresses the recently proposed reliability paradox (a phenomenon where a cognitive paradigm exhibits stable experimental effects at the group level, but is unstable at the individual level). It collected 42 datasets (from a total of 22 articles) to examine the reliability of a self-prioritization effect paradigm (self-matching task). Additionally, this paper also examined the reliability of six indices: reaction time (RT), accuracy, efficiency (reaction time / accuracy), d-prime from Signal Detection Theory, and drift rate (v) and start point (z) from the Drift Diffusion Model.

Responsibility:

Emailed authors to request raw data from papers that utilized the self-matching task.
Utilized dplyr and tidyr to clean the raw data.
Developed two R packages (yukiSH & yukiBP) for splitting the raw data into two halves to calculate split-half reliability across six indices in this paradigm.
Conducted a classic meta-analysis using metafor to demonstrate the robustness of the experimental effect across papers.
Visualized the results using ggplot2.
Authored the original draft.




Project 5

A Meta-analytical Comparison of the Self Prioritization Effect.


 GitHub  OSF  DOI

This meta-analysis aims to quantify the overall Self-Prioritization Effect (SPE) observed in associative learning tasks, such as the Self-Matching Task and the Ownership paradigm. It will investigate the magnitude, generalizability, and specificity of the SPE, exploring how its effect size varies across different cognitive processes and identifying potential moderators including associative learning task types, baseline conditions, individual differences, experimental procedures, and publication-related factors.

Responsibility:

Trained recruited coders and assigned coding tasks.
Coded collected articles, extracting key information.
Conducted a traditional meta-analysis using metafor.
Visualized the results using ggplot2.
Authored the original draft.




Project 6

The Heterogeneity of Youth Depression Scales


 GitHub  OSF  DOI

Role: Contributor
This study systematically examined the heterogeneity of depression scales for Chinese children and adolescents. Across 27 scales, we found substantial differences in symptom coverage and low overlap between instruments. These findings suggest that youth depression scales are not interchangeable and highlight the need for culturally and developmentally adapted assessment tools in non-Western contexts.

Responsibility: I contributed to the early-stage coding work and visualized the differences in what the scales measure.



Project 7

Business Decision-making Game Facilitates Training Effectiveness: A Three-level Meta‑Analysis


 GitHub  DOI

Role: Contributor
This three-level meta-analysis of 41 studies (N = 8376) reveals that business decision-making games significantly enhance training effectiveness with a moderate overall effect (g = 0.53). These positive outcomes remain robust across various participant types, game designs, and academic fields, supporting the broad implementation of such games in business education.

Responsibility: I was responsible for developing the standardized workflow code for the meta-analysis.

title: multiRL
text:
Overview
This package modularizes the Markov Decision Process (MDP) into six core components, enabling users to flexibly construct the Rescorla-Wagner Model for Multi-Armed Bandit tasks (see Sutton & Barto, 2018). Beginners can define models using simple if-else logic, making model construction more accessible (built-in three basic models, see Niv et al., 2012).

Step 1: Build Reinforcement Learning Models run_m()
Step 2: Parameter and Model Recovery rcv_d()
Step 3: Fit Real Data fit_p()
Step 4: Replay the Experiment rpl_e()

These four steps follow the ten simple rules for the computational modeling of behavioral data (Wilson & Collins 2019)

# Load package
library(multiRL)
# Obtain help document
?multiRL

Multiple Choices
Obviously, this package supports multi-choice tasks. In addition, we do not know what humans treat as the target when they encounter a particular state and update their values, especially when the cue and the response are not the same. In such cases, the agent typically needs to learn latent rules.



behrule = list(
  cue = c("Red", "Yellow", "Green", "Blue"),
  rsp = c("Up", "Down", "Left", "Right")
)


Multiple Systems
When humans make decisions, multiple cognitive processing systems may be involved (e.g., RL, WM, …). Each cognitive system may update its own Q-value representation, and these multiple Q-value estimates are then combined with different weights to influence the final choice.



system = c("RL", "WM", "...")


Multiple Modules



# learning-rate function
lrng_func = multiRL::func_alpha
\[
  Q_{new} = Q_{old} + \alpha \cdot (R - Q_{old})  
\]
# soft-max function  
prob_func = multiRL::func_beta
\[
  P_{t}(a) =
    \frac{
      \exp\left( \beta \cdot \left( Q_t(a) - \max_{j} Q_t(a_j) \right) \right)
    }{
      \sum_{i=1}^{k} \exp\left(
        \beta \cdot \left( Q_t(a_i) - \max_{j} Q_t(a_j) \right) \right
      )
    }
\]
# utility function
util_func = multiRL::func_gamma
\[
  U(R) = {R}^{\gamma}
\]
# bias function (upper-confidence-bound, sticky, ...)
bias_func = multiRL::func_delta
\[
  \text{Bias} = \delta \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\log(N + e)}{N + 10^{-10}}}
\]
# exploration function (ε-first, ε-greedy, ε-decrasing)  
expl_func = multiRL::func_epsilon
\[
  P(x) =
    \begin{cases}
      \epsilon, & x=1  \\
      1-\epsilon, & x=0
    \end{cases}
\]
# decay function (working memory)
dcay_func = multiRL::func_zeta
\[
  W_{new} = W_{old} + \zeta \cdot (W_{0} - W_{old})
\]

title: A multiverse assessment of the reliability of the self‑matching task as a measurement of the self‑prioritization effect
text:
The self-matching task (SMT) has become a widely adopted paradigm for investigating the self-prioritization effect (SPE), consistently demonstrating a robust processing advantage for self-associated stimuli. To quantify this robustness, we synthesized 42 independent datasets (\(N = 2250\)) using a meta-analytical approach. Our results confirmed that the SPE is a highly stable experimental effect at the group level, exhibiting moderate to large effect sizes across nearly all examined measures.



Despite its group-level stability, the SMT exhibits a notable reliability paradox when evaluated for individual differences. In our assessment of six key metrics—reaction time (RT), accuracy (ACC), efficiency (\(\eta\)), sensitivity (\(d'\)), and the drift-diffusion model (DDM) parameters \(v\) and \(z\)—we found generally low split-half reliability. Among these, RT and efficiency emerged as the most relatively reliable indicators, though their coefficients still hovered around an unsatisfactory level of approximately \(0.5\).



Since trial counts vary significantly across studies, we utilized the Spearman-Brown prediction formula to estimate the number of observations required to achieve a “good” reliability threshold of \(0.8\). Our predictions indicate that while RT requires approximately \(170\) trials to reach this level, other metrics require substantially more. Notably, the reliability for DDM-derived parameters was exceptionally poor, with the starting point (\(z\)) near zero, suggesting that the standard DDM may not be an appropriate fit for the cognitive architecture of the SMT.



In addition, to identify the most effective computational tools for this paradigm, we performed parameter recovery tests on simulated data. We observed significant discrepancies in recovery accuracy among various R packages. After comparing five different algorithms, we determined that the RWiener package provided the most favorable balance of accuracy and computational efficiency, outperforming other R packages.

title: binaryRL: Reinforcement Learning Modeling of Two-Alternative Forced Choice Decision Making in R — A Step-by-Step Tutorial
text:
binaryRL is built upon the foundational four-step framework (Wilson & Collins, 2019) for computational modeling. This provides a systematic roadmap that ensures methodological rigor throughout the entire process, from model construction to result reporting. To facilitate immediate use, the package includes three pre-built, canonical reinforcement learning models as described by Niv et al. (2012).

 

Researchers need only understand the interaction between the core components of a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to begin building their own tailored models. By utilizing familiar if-else logic to define custom cognitive processes, users can bypass the steep learning curve traditionally associated with coding reinforcement learning from scratch. The entire modeling workflow is streamlined into four key functions: run_m() for core model execution, rcv_d() for parameter and model recovery, fit_p() for fitting real data, and rpl_e() for replaying experimental effects.
